name: Vinotherapy

card.summary: Spa and skincare treatments using grapes, grape seeds and wine residue, aimed at exfoliating skin and giving a smoother, younger-looking complexion.
card.note: Possible irritation or allergy to grape-derived products.

quick.overview:
Vinotherapy is a beauty treatment in which the by-products of winemaking, such as grape pips, pulp and extracts, are applied to the skin through scrubs, wraps, baths and creams. The goal is smoother, brighter-looking skin and a reduction in visible signs of aging.

The modern form is tied to the French brand Caudalie, launched in 1995 by Mathilde and Bertrand Thomas after they learned about grape-seed polyphenols from a researcher. The claims rest on the antioxidant properties of grape polyphenols; no clinical studies of spa vinotherapy appear in the reference literature.
quick.how: People experience it as a spa service (grape-seed scrubs, wine or grape baths, wraps) or use grape- and vine-based skincare products at home. Spa sessions are one-off treatments, and cosmetic lines are used as part of a daily routine.
quick.risks: Grape-derived products are generally topical and low risk, but irritation or allergic reactions are possible, and heated baths or scrubs may not suit sensitive skin. Marketing claims about anti-aging are not backed by trials of the treatment itself.

lead: Vinotherapy is a beauty and spa practice that uses winemaking by-products, mainly grape pips and pulp, rubbed into or applied to the skin. The pulp is claimed to exfoliate, and the products are marketed as reducing visible aging.[1]

The commercial form of the practice is associated with Caudalie. Mathilde and Bertrand Thomas learned about grape seeds from polyphenol researcher Dr. Vercauteren and in 1995 launched a skincare line based on them; the company is credited with the first stabilized, patented extraction of grape-seed polyphenols (OPC) for cosmetic use.[1]

The approach appears in spas that offer wine-themed treatments, including a vinothérapie spa hotel in La Rioja, Spain.[1] Published clinical research on the spa treatment itself is not summarized in the main encyclopedia entry.[1]

chain: Grape seed and pulp scrubs and polyphenol creams are applied
Exfoliation and antioxidant ingredients are claimed to smooth and protect skin
angle.text: People use vinotherapy to get a smoother, more radiant-looking complexion. The exfoliating action of scrubs is immediate; the anti-aging benefits are claimed on the basis of grape polyphenols.

infobox: Grape pips, pulp, vine and grape-seed extracts

paras: Treatments include scrubs using crushed grape seeds and pulp, wraps and baths, and topical creams containing grape-seed polyphenols.[1] Spas present them as a way to use the antioxidant-rich parts of the grape.

Caudalie's founders say the idea grew from learning about grape-seed polyphenols from a researcher, leading to the 1995 line of products and later spa locations.[1] The term vinothérapie is now also used by wine-region hotels and spas elsewhere in Europe.[1]
Proponents say grape polyphenols act as antioxidants that protect skin and that the pulp exfoliates it, leaving skin visibly smoother and younger.[1]
No studies found for vinotherapy spa treatments as such. Research on grape-seed polyphenols as antioxidants is a separate, broader field.

timeline.event: Mathilde and Bertrand Thomas launch the Caudalie skincare line based on grape-seed polyphenols.[1]
